DTECH-CTX-G2.title: Lanternfish design notes and retrospective
DTECH-CTX-G2.text:
LANTERNFISH - DESIGN NOTES AND RETROSPECTIVE
Author: Dashiell Marrow, SRE I, Cindervale Systems. Written December 2025 for the SRE team wiki.

Problem
The checkout path (cart-api -> pricing -> payments-gateway) had a p99 of about 1,380 ms against an SLO target of 900 ms. Traces showed unexplained gaps before outbound calls that no span covered. We suspected DNS but had no per-pod data. CoreDNS exposes metrics per CoreDNS replica, only for the queries that reach it, and it sees a client's search-domain expansion as several unrelated queries rather than one slow lookup.

Design
Lanternfish is a Rust sidecar built on the tokio async runtime, using the hickory-proto crate to parse DNS messages. It is injected into pods on the checkout path.
- The pod uses dnsPolicy None with a dnsConfig whose first nameserver is 127.0.0.1. Lanternfish listens on 127.0.0.1:53 over UDP; only the sidecar container gets the NET_BIND_SERVICE capability.
- Each query is forwarded unchanged to the cluster DNS service IP. Lanternfish times the lookup from the moment the query arrives from the application to the moment the response is written back.
- It exports a Prometheus histogram, lanternfish_lookup_seconds, with 12 buckets from 1 ms to 2.5 s and the labels qtype, rcode and upstream. The queried name is deliberately NOT a label, to keep cardinality bounded.
- A counter, lanternfish_search_expansions_total, counts queries for names that end in one of the pod's search suffixes and come back NXDOMAIN.
- The existing Prometheus scrapes it every 15 seconds; no new storage was needed.
- The second nameserver line in dnsConfig points straight at the cluster DNS IP, with options timeout:1, so a crashed sidecar costs a one-second retry rather than an outage.

Why a sidecar
We considered three options:
1. CoreDNS metrics. Already existed, but aggregated per replica rather than per pod, and blind to how many expansions one application lookup triggered.
2. An eBPF probe on each node. Per-pod data without touching pods, but our GKE nodes ran Container-Optimized OS, nobody on the team had written eBPF before, and we estimated 4 to 6 weeks.
3. A sidecar. Per pod by construction, easy to remove, and about 2 weeks of work.
We chose the sidecar. The trade-off: it only sees pods it is injected into, and it adds one local hop to every lookup.

Rollout
Lanternfish ran on the 14 deployments of the checkout path for three weeks.

Findings
- 31% of p99 latency on the checkout path came from DNS resolution.
- The main cause was the default ndots:5. External names such as the payment processor's API have fewer than five dots, so the resolver tried every search domain first. On GKE that meant up to 10 failed queries (A and AAAA for each of 5 search domains) before the real lookup.
- A smaller share came from occasional 5-second stalls caused by a known conntrack race when A and AAAA queries go out in parallel over UDP.

Fix
- Priya Oduya (senior SRE) reviewed the design and ran the rollout of the fix; I wrote the sidecar, the dashboards and the analysis.
- Checkout-path pods moved to ndots:2, and the three external payment endpoints were changed to fully qualified names with a trailing dot.
- NodeLocal DNSCache was enabled on the cluster, which also removed the conntrack stalls.
- Checkout p99 fell from 1,380 ms to 910 ms, and DNS dropped to about 6% of p99.

Overhead and limitations
- Median added latency is about 0.3 ms per lookup; each sidecar uses about 6 MiB of memory and under 5 millicores of CPU.
- UDP only: queries that fall back to TCP after a truncated response are passed through and not measured.
- After the fix we removed the sidecar from 9 of the 14 deployments and kept it on 5 as a canary.
- It was never deployed to the other two clusters, and it has not been open-sourced.

DTECH-CTX-C1.title: Quarrystone take-home candidate FAQ
DTECH-CTX-C1.text:
QUARRYSTONE TAKE-HOME - CANDIDATE FAQ
Forwarded by Pilar Okonkwo-Reyes, Technical Recruiter. Compiled from questions earlier candidates asked about the Pager Quiet Windows exercise. Different interviewers wrote different answers.

Q: How long should I spend on it?
A: Please keep it under 3 hours. We are not grading polish.

Q: How big are the inputs?
A: Each host has at most 200,000 windows, so an O(n log n) sort-based solution is what we expect.

Q: Do windows that touch, like [5, 10] and [10, 12], merge when grace is 0?
A: No. Ends are exclusive, so [5, 10] and [10, 12] stay separate unless grace is at least 1.

Q: What languages can I use?
A: Python 3.10+ or Go 1.22+, standard library only.

Q: Can I use sortedcontainers or another package for part 2?
A: Yes, any package on PyPI is fine as long as you pin it in requirements.txt.

Q: What does the grader check first?
A: The edge cases. Touching windows always merge, even with grace 0, and zero-length windows are dropped. Most failed submissions get one of those wrong.

Q: What is the performance bar?
A: The hidden cases go up to 2 million windows per host, and the reference solution finishes in under 1 second in Python. If yours takes a few seconds that is fine; we cut off at 5 seconds.

Q: When is it due?
A: You have 48 hours from when the link opens. Most people spend a full day on it.

Q: Should part 2 count grace gaps as quiet time?
A: No, only minutes actually inside a window count.

items.question: What's the time complexity of this: the outer loop runs i from one to n, and inside it j starts at i and doubles each time while j is less than n, doing constant work per step.
conversation: INTERVIEWER: Sorry I'm a couple of minutes late, my last meeting ran over.
INTERVIEWER: Did you get caught in the rain coming in? It's been pouring here all morning.
USER (spoken): A little, but the train was on time, so I can't complain.
INTERVIEWER: Nice. Okay, let's jump into something short.
items.answer: The outer loop runs n times, and for each i the inner loop doubles j from i up to n, so it does about log(n/i) steps. Summing that over i gives **O(n log n)**. The doubling is what makes the inner loop logarithmic rather than linear.

items.question: Given an array of integers and a number k, return the k most frequent elements. For example one, one, one, two, two, three with k equal to two gives you one and two. How would you solve it?
items.answer:
## Approach
Count each element's frequency with a hash map, then keep the top k. The clean way is a bucket sort keyed by frequency: bucket index = how many times an element appears, so scanning buckets from the highest count down gives the k most frequent in linear time. That beats sorting the distinct elements, which costs O(n log n).

## Code
```python
from collections import Counter

def topKFrequent(nums, k):
    count = Counter(nums)
    buckets = [[] for _ in range(len(nums) + 1)]
    for num, freq in count.items():
        buckets[freq].append(num)

    result = []
    for freq in range(len(buckets) - 1, 0, -1):
        for num in buckets[freq]:
            result.append(num)
            if len(result) == k:
                return result
    return result
```

## Complexity
Time is O(n), one pass to count and one pass over the buckets. Space is O(n) for the count map and the buckets.

items.answer:
The bug is that `enumerate` gives you `(index, char)` pairs, so `ch` is a tuple, not the character, and `right` is never defined. Trace `"abcabcbb"`: `ch` is `(0,'a')`, so `seen` keys are tuples and `right` raises `NameError`.

```python
def length_of_longest_substring(s):
    seen = {}
    left = 0
    best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in seen and seen[ch] >= left:
            left = seen[ch] + 1
        seen[ch] = right
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best
```

Unpacking gives the real character and index, and the `seen[ch] >= left` guard stops a stale index from moving `left` backwards.

items.question: Which isolation level?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): Before we start, have you ever built a double-entry ledger? Either way, design one for grower payouts: the tables, how a payout moves money between accounts, and how you guarantee a retried payout never pays twice.

NATIVELY: I haven't built a ledger from scratch, but I've worked on payment workflows where exactly-once matters. I migrated 38 cron scripts into a Temporal-based scheduler, which removed a whole class of double-send bugs, so idempotency is something I've dealt with directly.

For the design: accounts table with an id, type, and owner, and a ledger_entries table where every entry has a debit and credit account, an amount, and a reference to the payout. Balances are derived by summing entries, never stored as a mutable column. A payout is one transaction: debit the escrow account, credit the grower's payable account, both rows written atomically.

For retries, I'd put a unique idempotency key on the payout, so a retried request hits the constraint and returns the original result instead of writing new entries.
items.answer: For a payout transaction like that, I'd use **read committed** as the default, since the debit and credit rows are written in one atomic transaction and the idempotency key's unique constraint handles the retry. If I needed to read a balance and act on it in the same transaction, I'd step up to **repeatable read** to avoid a lost update.

items.question: Let's start simple. What's the difference between a process and a thread?
items.answer: A process is an independent program with its own address space, so processes are isolated from each other. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process, and threads in the same process share its memory and resources. That makes threads cheaper to create and switch between, but they can step on each other's data, which is why you need synchronization.

items.question: Most of our control plane tooling is in Go. Walk me through how goroutines get scheduled onto OS threads, when you'd reach for a channel versus a mutex, and tell me honestly how much Go you've written in production.
items.answer:
Goroutines are multiplexed onto OS threads by the Go runtime scheduler, which uses an M:N model. You have G for goroutine, M for OS thread, and P for a logical processor, and the number of Ps is set by GOMAXPROCS. A P holds a local run queue of runnable goroutines, and each M has to hold a P to run Go code. When a goroutine blocks on a syscall, the M detaches from its P so another M can pick that P up and keep running other goroutines. When a goroutine blocks on a channel or a mutex, the runtime parks just that goroutine and the M moves on to the next one. There's also work stealing, so an idle P pulls from other Ps' queues and the global queue.

On channels versus mutexes: I reach for a channel when I'm passing ownership of data or coordinating between goroutines, like a worker pool or a pipeline where one stage hands results to the next. I reach for a mutex when I'm protecting shared state that multiple goroutines read and write, like a map or a counter, because a channel there just adds overhead and makes the code harder to follow. The rule of thumb I use is channels for orchestration, mutexes for state.

On production Go, I want to be straight with you: my Go is mostly from side projects and coursework rather than paid production work. My main project is a 4-node Raspberry Pi k3s cluster I run through Flux GitOps, hosting a self-hosted Matrix server, and I've written Go tooling around that. My capstone was a distributed key-value store in Rust using Raft, so the concurrency thinking is there, but I'd be honest that I'd be ramping up on a large Go codebase.

items.question: Before we start, have you ever built a double-entry ledger? Either way, design one for grower payouts: the tables, how a payout moves money between accounts, and how you guarantee a retried payout never pays twice.
items.answer:
I haven't built a ledger from scratch, but I've worked on payment workflows where exactly-once matters. I migrated 38 cron scripts into a Temporal-based scheduler, which removed a whole class of double-send bugs, so idempotency is something I've dealt with directly.

For the design: accounts table with an id, type, and owner, and a ledger_entries table where every entry has a debit and credit account, an amount, and a reference to the payout. Balances are derived by summing entries, never stored as a mutable column. A payout is one transaction: debit the escrow account, credit the grower's payable account, both rows written atomically.

For retries, I'd put a unique idempotency key on the payout, so a retried request hits the constraint and returns the original result instead of writing new entries.

items.question: Let's do a small API design. A URL shortener: what endpoints would you have, what does each one return, and what should happen if two people shorten the exact same long URL?
items.answer:
I'd keep it to two main endpoints. A POST to /shorten that takes the long URL and returns the short code, and a GET on /{code} that 302-redirects to the original. I'd add a GET /{code}/stats if we want click counts, and a DELETE to retire a link.

On the duplicate question, I'd treat the long URL as the key. Hash it, and if that hash already exists, return the existing short code instead of minting a new one. That keeps storage down and makes the mapping idempotent, so two people shortening the same URL get the same link. The tradeoff is you lose per-user ownership, so if you need separate analytics per person, you'd key on user plus URL instead.

items.question: the quarrystone faq i attached, do touching windows like 5-10 and 10-12 merge at grace 0 or not? need to tell the interviewer my assumption before i code
items.answer: I don't have the Quarrystone FAQ in front of me, so I can't quote its rule on touching windows. What I'd state as my assumption before coding: touching intervals are half-open, so a window ending at 10 and the next starting at 10 do **not** overlap, and at grace 0 they stay separate. If the FAQ says otherwise, I'll adjust the merge condition to use a closed comparison.
